  • Reduces thrust
  • Causes vibration

3. Spot Cavitation:

  • Localized patches
  • Occurs on blade surface
  • Less severe
  • Can cause pitting

Q.2(b) - Rolling Decrement

Definition: The decrement is the reduction in roll amplitude from one oscillation to the next.

Graph:

Amplitude
    ↑
    │  ╲    ╲    ╲
    │   ╲    ╲    ╲
    │    ╲    ╲    ╲
    │     ╲    ╲    ╲
    │      ╲    ╲    ╲
    └────────────────→ Time

Causes of Reduction in Still Water:

  1. Wave resistance of motion
  2. Skin friction damping
  3. Eddy making resistance
  4. Added mass effects

Q.3 - Damaged Box-Shaped Vessel

Given:

  • L = 280 m, B = 22 m
  • Draft = 7 m
  • 4 transverse bulkheads + 1 longitudinal = 10 compartments
  • GM = 3.0 m

Flooding condition: Forwardmost port compartment flooded

Step 1: Flooded volume

Compartment dimensions from arrangement Flooded volume calculation using permeability

Step 2: Added mass

Mass of floodwater = Volume × permeability × density

Step 3: New draft and trim

Using lost buoyancy method Calculate sinkage and trim

Step 4: Drafts at corners

FP, FS, AP, AS drafts calculated Using trim and heel

Q.4(a) - Triangular Bulkhead Thrust

Given:

  • Depth = 15 m
  • Breadth = 18 m at top
  • Sounding = 17 m

Step 1: Triangular area

Area = (1/2) × 18 × 15 = 135 m²

Step 2: Center of pressure

For triangle with apex down: COP from apex = 3h/4 from top = 3 × 15/4 = 11.25 m from top = 3.75 m from bottom

Step 3: Thrust

If sounding = 17 m, water extends beyond bulkhead T = ρ × g × A × h_avg

h_avg = depth to centroid from surface

Q.4(b) - Oil Tanker vs Dry Cargo Ship

Tanker Design Strengths:

  1. Stresses:

    • Longitudinal strength
    • Transverse bulkheads
    • Deep transverse frames

  2. Stability Advantages:

    • Wide beam
    • Low KG
    • Large GM

  3. ILLC Freeboard Considerations:

    • Reduced freeboard allowed
    • Type A vessel status
    • High deck openings protected

Q.6 - Safe Return to Port Discussion

SRtP Requirements:

  1. Redundancy:

    • Propulsion systems
    • Steering systems
    • Auxiliary systems

  2. Fire protection:

    • Enhanced fire-fighting
    • Structural fire protection

  3. Flooding protection:

    • Subdivision
    • Pumping capacity

Objectives:

  1. Reduce evacuation need
  2. Return to port unassisted
  3. Maintain safety functions
  4. Protect passengers and crew

Implementation:

  • System redundancy
  • Damage control planning
  • Training requirements
  • Documentation

2025 EM202 SOLUTIONS

Q.1(a) - Tapered Beam SF and BM

Given:

  • L = 10 m
  • A₁ = 6 m² (free end)
  • A₂ = 16 m² (fixed end)
  • ρ = 0.8 kg/m³

Step 1: Area variation

Area at distance x from free end: A(x) = 6 + (10x/10) = 6 + x (since taper is uniform)

Step 2: Weight distribution

w(x) = ρ × A(x) × g = 0.8 × (6 + x) × 9.81 = 7.848(6 + x) N/m

Step 3: Shear force

S(x) = ∫₀ˣ w(x) dx = 7.848(6x + x²/2)

Step 4: Bending moment

M(x) = ∫₀ˣ S(x) dx = 7.848(3x² + x³/6)

Shear Force Diagram:

S
↑
│  ╲
│   ╲
│    ╲
│     ╲
│      ╲
└───────→ x

Bending Moment Diagram:

M
↑
│    _____
│   /
│  /
│ /
│/
└─────→ x

Q.1(b) - Box Vessel Damage (Repeat of 2021 Q.1)

[Same as 2021 Q.1 solution]

Q.2(a) - Simpson’s Rules Derivation

Simpson’s First Rule:

For n even and equal intervals: ∫₀^(nh) f(x) dx = (h/3)(f₀ + 4f₁ + 2f₂ + 4f₃ + … + 4f_{n-1} + f_n)

Derivation:

Using quadratic interpolation between three points: f(x) = ax² + bx + c

Integrating over 2h: ∫₀^(2h) f(x) dx = (h/3)(f₀ + 4f₁ + f₂)

Simpson’s Second Rule:

For n = 3 intervals: ∫₀^(3h) f(x) dx = (3h/8)(f₀ + 3f₁ + 3f₂ + f₃)

Q.2(b) - Moment of Inertia Derivation

Moment of inertia about y-axis:

I_y = ∫ x² dA dA = y dx

Therefore: I_y = ∫ y x² dx

This is the second moment of area about the y-axis.

Q.3 - Structural Terms Explanation

Bending Moment:

  • Sum of moments about neutral axis
  • Causes bending stress
  • M = ∫σ×y×dA

Neutral Axis:

  • Line of zero stress
  • Where bending strains are zero
  • Passes through centroid

Bending Stress:

  • σ = M × y / I
  • Varies linearly from neutral axis
  • Maximum at extreme fibers

Hull Deflection:

  • Vertical displacement of hull
  • Occurs due to bending
  • Measured at mid-length

Section Modulus:

  • Z = I / y_max
  • Measures resistance to bending
  • Larger Z = stronger section

Second Moment of Area:

  • I = ∫ y² dA
  • Measures distribution of area
  • Determines bending stiffness

Interrelationship:

  • Stress = Moment / Section Modulus
  • Deflection ∝ Moment / (E × I)
  • All related through beam theory

Q.4 - Propeller Calculations (Repeat of 2019 Q.2)

[Same as 2019 Q.2 solution]

Q.5(a) - Ship Model Resistance

Given:

  • Model length: 6 m
  • Wetted surface: 7 m²
  • Speed: 3 knots
  • Resistance: 35 N
  • Ship length: 120 m
  • n = 1.825
  • SCF = 1.15

Step 1: Scale ratio

λ = L_ship / L_model = 120/6 = 20

Step 2: Speed scaling

V_ship = V_model × √λ = 3 × √20 = 13.42 knots

Step 3: Resistance scaling

R_ship = R_model × λ^n × SCF = 35 × 20^1.825 × 1.15 = 35 × 244 × 1.15 = 9,821 N

Step 4: Total resistance

R_total = 9,821 × 1.15 = 11,294 N

Q.5(b) - Frictional Resistance Dependence

1. Length:

  • Increases with L (R_f ∝ L^0.8-1.0)
  • Due to increased wetted surface
  • Longer ships have higher resistance

2. Speed:

  • R_f ∝ V^n where n ≈ 1.825-1.9
  • Increases non-linearly
  • Major component at high speed

3. Wetted Surface Area:

  • Directly proportional
  • More area = more friction
  • Affected by hull form

4. Hull Roughness:

  • Increased roughness = increased friction
  • Corrosion and fouling increase resistance
  • Requires regular maintenance

Q.6 - Industrial Personnel Code (Repeat of 2020 Q.2(b))

[Same as 2020 Q.2(b) solution]

End of Solutions

item.title: IMO Fire Safety Regulations-Layers of Protection & SOLAS Chapter II-2
item.description:
1. Layers of Protection in Fire Safety (IMO Approach)

The IMO’s fire safety philosophy is based on four layers of protection, designed to address fire at every stage:

Layer Objective Key Measures (SOLAS Ch. II-2)
Prevention Minimize the probability of fire ignition. - Restrictions on ignition sources (e.g., electrical equipment, hot work permits).- Use of non-combustible materials in construction.- Smoking restrictions in cargo holds and accommodation spaces.
Fire Spread Prevention Limit the spread of fire if ignition occurs. - Structural fire divisions (A, B, C class bulkheads/decks).- Fire doors (self-closing, fire-rated).- Fire dampers in ventilation systems.- Thermal insulation to delay heat transfer.
Fire Extinction Detect and extinguish fires effectively. - Fixed fire extinguishing systems (CO₂, foam, water mist).- Portable extinguishers (dry chemical, foam, CO₂).- Fire main system (hose reels, hydrants).- Automatic sprinklers in accommodation spaces.
Safety of Life Ensure safe evacuation and survival of crew and passengers. - Emergency escape routes (protected, illuminated).- Firefighter’s outfits and breathing apparatus.- Lifesaving appliances (lifeboats, liferafts).- Fire drills and training.

2. Fire Safety Objectives, Functional Requirements & SOLAS Ch. II-2

A. Fire Safety Objectives (IMO)

The primary objectives of IMO’s fire safety regulations are:

  1. Prevent fire occurrence (minimize ignition sources).
  2. Limit fire growth (contain fire to the compartment of origin).
  3. Ensure structural integrity (prevent collapse due to fire).
  4. Facilitate evacuation (safe escape routes).
  5. Enable fire suppression (effective extinguishing systems).
  6. Protect adjacent spaces (prevent fire spread).

B. Functional Requirements (SOLAS Ch. II-2)

SOLAS Chapter II-2 (Fire Protection, Fire Detection, and Fire Extinction) is performance-based, meaning it specifies what must be achieved rather than how to achieve it. The functional requirements include:

Functional Requirement Purpose Example Regulations in SOLAS Ch. II-2
Containment of Fire Fire must be contained within the compartment of origin for a specified time. - A-60, B-15, C-0 class divisions (Reg. 9).- Fire doors (Reg. 9.4).- Fire dampers (Reg. 9.7).
Limitation of Fire Spread Prevent fire from spreading to adjacent compartments. - Structural fire integrity (Reg. 9).- Thermal insulation (Reg. 9.2).- Non-combustible materials (Reg. 3).
Extinction of Fire Provide means to detect and extinguish fires. - Fixed fire extinguishing systems (Reg. 10).- Portable extinguishers (Reg. 10.2).- Fire main system (Reg. 10.1).
Protection of Escape Routes Ensure safe evacuation in case of fire. - Protected escape routes (Reg. 13).- Emergency lighting (Reg. 13.3).- Low-location lighting (Reg. 13.3.2).
Structural Integrity Maintain ship’s structural strength during and after a fire. - Fire resistance ratings (A-60, B-15, etc.).- Load-bearing capacity (Reg. 9.2.2).

3. Specialty of SOLAS Chapter II-2 Arrangement

SOLAS Chapter II-2 is unique because it:

  1. Adopts a Performance-Based Approach:
    • Specifies objectives and functional requirements rather than prescriptive solutions.
    • Allows innovative designs (e.g., alternative fire suppression systems) if they meet the same safety level.
  2. Incorporates Risk-Based Design:
    • Fire Risk Assessment (FRA) can be used to justify alternative arrangements (Reg. 17).
    • Encourages design improvements (e.g., safe return to port concept).
  3. Covers All Ship Types:
    • Applies to passenger ships, cargo ships, and tankers with specific amendments for each.
  4. Regularly Updated:
    • Amendments incorporate lessons from incidents (e.g., Scandinavian Star, Emma Maersk).

4. Structural Fire Divisions on a Ship

A. Types of Fire Divisions (SOLAS Reg. 9)

Structural fire divisions are classified based on their fire resistance and ability to prevent fire spread. The three main classes are:

Class Fire Resistance Rating Purpose Typical Applications
A-0 0 minutes No fire resistance (used for non-critical spaces). Store rooms, non-essential spaces.
A-15 15 minutes Low fire resistance (delays fire spread). Corridors, stairways (in some cases).
A-30 30 minutes Moderate fire resistance. Accommodation bulkheads, some cargo holds.
A-60 60 minutes High fire resistance (prevents fire spread for 60 mins). Primary fire divisions (e.g., between cargo holds and accommodation).
B-0 0 minutes Non-combustible materials but no insulation. External bulkheads (non-load-bearing).
B-15 15 minutes Non-combustible + insulation (delays temperature rise). Some machinery spaces.
C Non-combustible No fire resistance rating but non-combustible (e.g., steel). Decks in open areas, non-fire-risk spaces.

B. Purpose of Structural Fire Divisions

  1. Contain Fire: Prevent fire from spreading beyond the compartment of origin.
  2. Delay Fire Spread: Provide time for evacuation and firefighting.
  3. Protect Critical Spaces: Shield accommodation, control stations, and escape routes.
  4. Maintain Structural Integrity: Ensure the ship does not collapse during a fire.

5. Fire Bulkheads and Decks: Testing Methods

A. Standard Fire Test (SOLAS Reg. 3.2)

The standard fire test evaluates the fire resistance of bulkheads and decks. It involves:

  1. Exposure to a Standard Fire Curve:
    • A time-temperature curve simulating a fully developed fire.
    • Temperature rises according to the formula: T = 345 log₁₀(8t + 1), where t = time in minutes.
  2. Criteria for Passing:
    • Integrity: No flames or hot gases pass through.
    • Insulation: Temperature rise on the unexposed side does not exceed:
      • 140°C above ambient (average).
      • 180°C above ambient (at any point).
    • Load-bearing capacity: Must withstand mechanical stress during the test.

B. Non-Combustibility Test (SOLAS Reg. 3.1)

  • Purpose: Ensure materials do not contribute to fire spread.
  • Test Method (ISO 1182):
    • A small sample is exposed to 750°C for 5 minutes in a furnace.
    • Passing Criteria:
      • No flame propagation.
      • Temperature rise ≤ 30°C in the furnace.
      • Weight loss ≤ 50% of the original sample.

6. Standard Fire Curve

A. Sketch of the Standard Fire Curve 

Time (minutes) | Temperature (°C)
----------------|------------------
0              | 20 (Ambient)
5              | ~576°C
10             | ~706°C
30             | ~842°C
60             | ~945°C
120            | ~1000°C

B. Significance of the Standard Fire Curve

  • Simulates a fully developed fire in a compartment.
  • Used to test fire resistance of bulkheads, decks, and doors.
  • Ensures consistent testing worldwide (IMO standardized).
  • Real-world relevance: Mimics cellulosic fires (e.g., wood, paper, textiles).

7. Case Study: Scandinavian Star (1990)

A. Incident Overview

  • Date: April 7, 1990.
  • Ship: Scandinavian Star (passenger/vehicle ferry).
  • Casualties: 159 deaths (one of the deadliest maritime disasters in peacetime).
  • Cause: Fire originated in a car deck, spread rapidly due to:
    • Inadequate fire divisions (B-class bulkheads instead of A-class).
    • Poor fire detection (no sprinklers in car decks).
    • Delayed evacuation (smoke spread to accommodation via ventilation systems).
    • Failure of fire doors (not self-closing).

B. Lessons Learned & SOLAS Amendments

  1. Stricter Fire Division Requirements:
    • Car decks now require A-60 class divisions (previously B-0 or B-15).
  2. Improved Fire Detection:
    • Automatic sprinklers mandatory in car decks and special category spaces (Reg. 10.2.1.3).
  3. Enhanced Ventilation Control:
    • Fire dampers must automatically close in case of fire (Reg. 9.7).
  4. Better Escape Routes:
    • Protected stairways and low-location lighting (Reg. 13).
  5. Human Element:
    • Mandatory fire drills and crew training (SOLAS Ch. II-2/15).

8. Significance of Insulation and Cable Penetrations in Fire Bulkheads/Decks

A. Insulation

  • Purpose:
    • Delays heat transfer to the unexposed side of the bulkhead/deck.
    • Prevents fire spread by maintaining temperature rise limits (140°C avg, 180°C max).
  • Materials:
    • Mineral wool, ceramic fiber, or calcium silicate (non-combustible).
  • Case Study: Emma Maersk (2006)
    • Issue: Fire in engine room spread via unprotected cable penetrations.
    • Lesson: Cable penetrations must be sealed with fire-resistant materials (e.g., fire-stopping systems).
    • SOLAS Requirement: Reg. 9.2.3 mandates fire-resistant sealing for all penetrations.

B. Cable Penetrations

  • Risk: Fire can spread through gaps where cables pass through bulkheads/decks.
  • Solution:
    • Fire-stopping systems (e.g., intumescent seals, fire-resistant putty).
    • Tested to the same fire resistance as the bulkhead (e.g., A-60 penetration = A-60 seal).
  • Emma Maersk Incident (2006):
    • Fire spread from the engine room to accommodation via unprotected cable penetrations.
    • Result: SOLAS amendments now require strict testing of cable transits (Reg. 9.2.3.2).

9. Design Innovations in Fire Safety

Modern ships incorporate innovative fire safety designs, such as:

Innovation Description Example/SOLAS Reference
Safe Return to Port (SRtP) Ships designed to return to port safely after a fire incident. SOLAS II-2/21 (for passenger ships).
Water Mist Systems Fine water spray extinguishes fire by cooling and oxygen displacement. Reg. 10.4 (allowed as an alternative to CO₂ in some spaces).
Fire-Resistant Composite Materials Lightweight, non-combustible materials (e.g., aluminum foam, fire-rated composites). Reg. 3 (non-combustibility requirements).
Advanced Fire Detection (AI/ML) AI-based fire detection (e.g., thermal cameras, smoke analysis). Reg. 7 (fire detection systems).
Modular Fireproofing Prefabricated fire-resistant panels for easier installation and maintenance. Used in modern cruise ships and LNG carriers.
Fire-Resistant Coatings Intumescent paints expand when exposed to heat, insulating steel structures. Reg. 9.2 (structural fire protection).

10. New Sections of SOLAS Chapter II-2

A. Design Improvements (Allowing for Innovation)

SOLAS Ch. II-2 includes new parts that allow for design improvements:

Part Focus Key Regulation
Part F Alternative Designs and Arrangements Reg. 17: Allows Fire Risk Assessment (FRA) to justify alternative designs.
Part G Special Requirements for Passenger Ships Reg. 18-20: Safe Return to Port (SRtP) and evacuation analysis.
Part H Fire Safety for Ships Carrying Dangerous Goods Reg. 19: Additional protections for LNG, LPG, and chemical tankers.
Part J Fire Safety Measures for Ships Using Low-Flashpoint Fuels Reg. 21: Addresses LNG-fueled ships and methane slip risks.

B. Human Element (Crew and Passenger Safety)

SOLAS Ch. II-2 also addresses the human element in fire safety:

Aspect SOLAS Regulation Purpose
Fire Drills Reg. 15.2.2 Mandatory weekly drills for crew.
Training Reg. 15.2.1 Firefighting training for all crew members.
Evacuation Plans Reg. 13.7 Clear escape route signage and muster station assignments.
Firefighter’s Outfits Reg. 10.10 Personal protective equipment (PPE) for firefighting teams.
Communication Reg. 10.6 Fire alarm systems with audible and visual signals.

11. Key Takeaways

  1. Layers of Protection: IMO’s approach ensures prevention, containment, extinction, and life safety.
  2. SOLAS Ch. II-2: Performance-based, allowing innovation while maintaining safety.
  3. Structural Fire Divisions: A-60, B-15, C-0 classifications ensure fire containment.
  4. Testing: Standard fire test and non-combustibility test validate fire resistance.
  5. Case Studies: Scandinavian Star (fire spread due to poor divisions) and Emma Maersk (cable penetrations) led to SOLAS amendments.
  6. Human Element: Training, drills, and evacuation plans are critical for fire safety.
  7. Design Innovations: Water mist, AI detection, and fire-resistant materials improve modern ship safety.

12. Discussion Questions

  1. How does the Fire Risk Assessment (FRA) process help in approving alternative fire safety designs?
  2. What are the challenges in implementing SRtP (Safe Return to Port) for existing ships?
  3. How do modern fire detection systems (e.g., AI-based) compare to traditional smoke detectors in terms of false alarms and response time?
  4. What lessons from the Emma Maersk fire can be applied to new ship designs?
  5. How does SOLAS Ch. II-2 balance prescriptive requirements with performance-based flexibility?

item.title: International Loadline Convention 1966-69-2005
item.description:
Under the International Convention on Load Lines, 1966 (as modified by the 1988 Protocol), the tabular freeboard is only the starting value. The final assigned summer freeboard is obtained by applying prescribed corrections and deductions that reflect hull form, depth, reserve buoyancy, strength, weathertight integrity, and the amount of enclosed superstructure. imorules

Q1. Corrections to tabulated freeboard

Starting point

  1. Determine the ship’s type:

    • Type A: usually tankers with high inherent weathertight integrity, small deck openings and good subdivision.
    • Type B: all ships that do not meet Type A conditions—most dry-cargo ships, container ships, bulk carriers and general-cargo ships.

  2. From the appropriate Type A or Type B table, obtain the tabular freeboard corresponding to the convention length LLL.

  3. Apply the relevant corrections in the specified order.

A typical calculation sequence for a Type B ship is:

[ \boxed{ F_{\text{assigned}}

F_{\text{tabular}} \pm C_{L<100} \pm C_{C_B} \pm C_D \pm C_{\text{deck line}}

  • D_{\text{superstructure/trunk}} \pm C_{\text{sheer}} } ]

Then verify:

Fassigned≥Fminimum F_{\text{assigned}} \geq F_{\text{minimum}} Fassigned​≥Fminimum​

and also check the separate minimum bow-height requirement.

Main corrections and their principles

Correction / deduction Effect on freeboard Underlying principle
Correction for ships under 100 m Usually increases Type B freeboard when the ship has little enclosed superstructure A short dry-cargo ship with limited enclosed volume has less reserve buoyancy and is more affected by waves; it needs greater protection than the basic table alone provides
Block-coefficient correction Increase if CB>0.68C_B > 0.68CB​>0.68; reduce if CB<0.68C_B < 0.68CB​<0.68, subject to limits A fuller ship has less buoyancy recovery as it heels or trims, greater exposure to green seas, and generally needs more reserve buoyancy. A finer ship has more favourable form characteristics and may receive a reduction
Depth correction Increase where actual depth exceeds the tabular/reference depth; may reduce where it is less, within limits Greater moulded depth gives more hull volume above the loaded waterline. The Convention gives credit for this reserve buoyancy, but only to a controlled extent and subject to minimum-freeboard rules
Correction for deck-line position Adjusts freeboard if the deck line is not at the normal intersection of freeboard deck and shell Freeboard is measured from the upper edge of the deck line. If the deck line is shifted from its normal datum, the numerical freeboard must be corrected so that the actual load line still represents the intended reserve buoyancy
Superstructure and trunk deduction Reduces freeboard Efficient enclosed superstructures and qualifying trunks create protected enclosed buoyancy above the freeboard deck, improve protection of deck openings, and reduce the likelihood of downflooding
Sheer correction Excess sheer reduces freeboard; deficiency increases it Sheer provides extra height, reserve buoyancy and protection at the ends, especially forward where green-sea boarding is severe. Deficient sheer removes this protection
Minimum bow-height check May require an increase in freeboard or bow height Adequate bow freeboard is needed to reduce deck wetness, green-water loading, hatch-cover damage and progressive flooding risk
Minimum freeboard check Prevents excessive reduction Regardless of deductions, the final assigned freeboard cannot be less than the Convention minimum applicable to the ship

The Convention chapter on freeboards specifically includes corrections for ships under 100 m, block coefficient, depth, deck-line position, superstructures/trunks, sheer, minimum bow height and minimum freeboards. imorules

Block coefficient correction

The block coefficient is:

CB=∇LBT C_B=\frac{\nabla}{LBT} CB​=LBT∇​

where:

  • ∇\nabla∇ = moulded displacement volume,
  • LLL = Convention length,
  • BBB = moulded breadth,
  • TTT = relevant moulded draught.

For a Type B ship, the standard reference form is approximately:

CB=0.68 C_B=0.68 CB​=0.68

The usual correction principle is:

CCB∝(CB−0.68) C_{C_B} \propto (C_B-0.68) CCB​​∝(CB​−0.68)

Therefore:

  • CB>0.68C_B>0.68CB​>0.68: add freeboard.
  • CB<0.68C_B<0.68CB​<0.68: deduct freeboard, subject to the permitted maximum deduction.

A full-bodied bulk carrier, for example, normally attracts an increase because it is more vulnerable to deck immersion and may have less favourable reserve-buoyancy characteristics than a finer vessel.

Depth correction

The relevant depth is the freeboard depth, measured amidships from keel to the top of the freeboard deck beam at side, including the thickness of the freeboard deck at side where applicable. assets.publishing.service.gov

A deeper ship possesses more potential enclosed buoyancy above the assigned waterline. Thus, subject to Convention limits:

  • Extra depth can justify a freeboard deduction.
  • Inadequate depth requires an addition.

However, additional depth alone must not be used to claim unsafe reductions where the vessel lacks proper structural strength, effective enclosure, closing appliances, or adequate stability. The Convention expressly assumes adequate structural strength, stability and avoidance of excessive structural stress at the assigned draught. assets.publishing.service.gov

Superstructure deduction

An enclosed superstructure is valuable because it creates reserve buoyancy that remains available when the vessel is deeply laden or heeled.

The deduction depends principally on:

EL \frac{E}{L} LE​

where:

  • EEE = total effective length of enclosed superstructures and qualifying trunks,
  • LLL = Convention length.

The more of the vessel’s length covered by effective enclosed superstructure, the greater the permitted deduction. If effective superstructure length equals the full ship length, the maximum applicable deduction is available; if it covers only part of the length, the deduction is proportionately smaller. laws-lois.justice.gc

Sheer correction

Sheer is treated separately because a raised deck line at the ends gives real safety benefit, especially in waves. The Convention correction is based on the difference between actual and standard sheer. A shortage of sheer generally increases freeboard; excess sheer may reduce it. assets.publishing.service.gov

Q2. Sheer: definition and calculation

Definition

Sheer is the longitudinal curvature of the freeboard deck measured at the ship’s side. It is the vertical distance between the actual deck line at side and a reference line drawn parallel to the keel through the sheer line amidships.

In simple terms:

  • The deck is lowest around midships.
  • It rises toward the bow and usually toward the stern.
  • The upward rise is called sheer.

The Convention measures sheer from the deck at side to a reference line parallel to the keel through the amidship sheer line. assets.publishing.service.gov

Simple sketch 

                  Actual freeboard-deck sheer line

      Forward                                          Aft
         ↑                                               ↑
         |                                               |
         |                                               |
     ____/ \_________________________________________/ \____
         \                                               /
          \_____________________________________________/
                Reference line through midships
                   parallel to the keel

                         Midships

At midships:

Sheer ordinate=0 \text{Sheer ordinate}=0 Sheer ordinate=0

At the ends, the vertical ordinate is at its maximum.

Standard sheer

For a normal ship, the standard sheer ordinates are expressed as fractions of LLL.

Position from nearest perpendicular Standard sheer ordinate
At FP or AP L50\dfrac{L}{50}50L​
At L6\dfrac{L}{6}6L​ from FP or AP L150\dfrac{L}{150}150L​
At L3\dfrac{L}{3}3L​ from FP or AP L500\dfrac{L}{500}500L​
Amidships 000

Thus, standard end sheer is:

Send=L50 S_{\text{end}}=\frac{L}{50} Send​=50L​

For example, if:

L=150 m L=150\ \text{m} L=150 m

then:

Send=15050=3.0 m S_{\text{end}}=\frac{150}{50}=3.0\ \text{m} Send​=50150​=3.0 m

So, at FP and AP, the standard freeboard-deck line is 3.0 m above the midship reference line.

Standard sheer sketch 

Forward end                                              Midships

      Standard end ordinate = L/50
                    ↑
                    │
                    │\
                    │ \
                    │  \
Reference line  ____│___\_______________________________
                  FP  L/6  L/3             0 at midships

Ordinate at FP      = L/50
Ordinate at L/6     = L/150
Ordinate at L/3     = L/500
Ordinate amidships  = 0

The same method is used aft, but the aft standard sheer is generally smaller than forward standard sheer for conventional freeboard calculations. This reflects the greater exposure of the bow to head seas and green-water loads.

Method of calculating actual sheer

For a newly built ship, calculate sheer separately at the forward and aft halves.

Step 1: Establish the reference line

Draw a straight line parallel to the keel through the deck line at side amidships.

             Freeboard deck at side
                  /
                 /
________________/___________________  Reference line
             midships

Step 2: Measure actual ordinates

At each side, measure the vertical distance from the reference line to the freeboard deck at:

  • Forward perpendicular, FP.
  • L/6L/6L/6 abaft FP.
  • L/3L/3L/3 abaft FP.
  • Amidships.
  • L/3L/3L/3 forward of AP.
  • L/6L/6L/6 forward of AP.
  • After perpendicular, AP.

The midship ordinate is normally zero.

FORWARD HALF

FP            L/6            L/3              Midships
|--------------|--------------|------------------|
↑              ↑              ↑                  ↑
S1             S2             S3                 0

Actual ordinates measured vertically from the
midship reference line to the deck at side.

Step 3: Compare with standard ordinates

At every station, find:

[ \text{Difference}= \text{Actual sheer ordinate}

\text{Standard sheer ordinate} ]

  • Positive result = excess sheer.
  • Negative result = deficient sheer.

Step 4: Calculate the mean excess or deficiency

The ordinates are not simply averaged; they are combined by the Convention’s prescribed weighting method. The midship region has no sheer ordinate, and the end sections are given appropriate significance because the protection near the ends—especially forward—is most important.

For examination purposes, state:

The actual and standard ordinates at FP/AP, L/6L/6L/6, and L/3L/3L/3 positions are compared. The excess or deficiency is integrated or weighted over the forward and aft halves in accordance with Regulation 38 to obtain the mean sheer excess or deficiency.

Step 5: Apply the correction

The Convention sheer correction is based on:

[ \text{Sheer correction}

(\text{mean deficiency or excess of sheer}) \times \text{applicable factor} ]

The factor depends upon the extent of effective enclosed superstructure. In the Convention text this is represented by a relationship involving the proportion of superstructure length; the correction reduces as the ship has more effective enclosed superstructure. assets.publishing.service.gov

Effect of superstructure on sheer credit

An enclosed superstructure itself provides reserve buoyancy and weather protection. Therefore, it may receive sheer credit if its actual height exceeds the standard superstructure height.

If a superstructure is higher than standard by ZZZ:

  • Add ZZZ to the end sheer ordinate.
  • Add 0.444Z0.444Z0.444Z at the L/6L/6L/6 station.
  • Add 0.111Z0.111Z0.111Z at the L/3L/3L/3 station.

These increments are applied at the relevant end. lk.rs-class

Extra superstructure height = Z

At end:       add Z
At L/6:       add 0.444 Z
At L/3:       add 0.111 Z
At midships:  add 0

How sheer improves safety and stability

Strictly speaking, sheer is primarily a reserve-buoyancy, seaworthiness and downflooding-protection feature rather than an initial-stability feature such as GMGMGM.

It contributes to safety in the following ways:

  • Increases hull volume above the loaded waterline at the bow and stern.
  • Increases reserve buoyancy as the end immerses due to waves, trim or heel.
  • Improves longitudinal restoring characteristics in pitching and trimming.
  • Reduces frequency of bow immersion and deck wetness.
  • Helps protect hatch covers, vents, doors and deck machinery from green-water impacts.
  • Reduces the likelihood of water accumulating in exposed wells or entering deck openings.
  • Improves the residual buoyancy margin at the ends after limited flooding.
Low-sheer vessel                     Vessel with adequate sheer

      Green water                          Green water
         ↓                                      ↓
 ________/\________                     _________/\_________
        /  \                                   /    \
_______/____\_______                    ______/______\_______
 Low forward reserve                    Greater forward reserve
 buoyancy; more wet deck                buoyancy; better protection

The key examination statement is:

Sheer does not usually create a large change in initial transverse GMGMGM, but it materially improves reserve buoyancy, the range of stability, resistance to deck immersion, longitudinal behaviour in waves, and protection against downflooding.

Limit on total deduction or addition

The assigned freeboard cannot be reduced without limit. The final value remains subject to:

  • Minimum-freeboard provisions.
  • Minimum bow-height requirements.
  • Adequate strength and intact stability.
  • Full compliance with the conditions of assignment: hatch closures, doors, ventilators, air pipes, freeing ports, guard rails, machinery-space protection, cargo ports and other opening protections.

The Convention allows a limited reduction from tabular freeboard when the vessel earns credit for favourable form, depth, enclosed superstructure, trunks and excess sheer; conversely, a vessel with unfavourable form, inadequate depth, deficient sheer or inadequate superstructure receives additions. The final assigned freeboard must never be below the prescribed minimum. imorules

Q3. Effective length of superstructure

Definition

The effective length of superstructure, denoted by EEE, is the length of an enclosed superstructure that is accepted for freeboard-deduction purposes.

It may be less than the actual geometrical length SSS, because the superstructure earns credit only to the extent that it provides meaningful enclosed buoyancy and weather protection.

                Actual length of enclosed superstructure = S

      ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │              Deckhouse / bridge          │
──────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┴──────
      <--------------- S ----------------------->

      <----------- E ----------->
      Effective length credited for freeboard

For an ordinary enclosed superstructure:

E=S E=S E=S

only where its height is at least the required standard superstructure height.

Standard superstructure height

The standard height is:

Hs=1.80+L300 H_s=1.80+\frac{L}{300} Hs​=1.80+300L​

in metres, with Convention limits for long ships.

For example, for a 150 m ship:

Hs=1.80+150300 H_s=1.80+\frac{150}{300} Hs​=1.80+300150​Hs=1.80+0.50 H_s=1.80+0.50 Hs​=1.80+0.50Hs=2.30 m \boxed{H_s=2.30\ \text{m}} Hs​=2.30 m​

So an enclosed 80 m bridge/deckhouse with an effective height of at least 2.30 m can usually receive full length credit:

E=S=80 m E=S=80\ \text{m} E=S=80 m

Why effective length is used

The reason is that not all structures of equal plan length give equal reserve buoyancy.

A tall, fully enclosed, strongly built, weathertight superstructure:

  • Adds real enclosed buoyancy.
  • Remains effective when the vessel heels.
  • Delays downflooding.
  • Protects openings on the freeboard deck.
  • Improves survivability in waves and damaged conditions.

A low or poorly enclosed deckhouse may provide less useful buoyancy and may be immersed or downflooded sooner. It should therefore not receive the same freeboard deduction.

High enclosed superstructure             Low superstructure

      ┌───────────────┐                   ┌───────────────┐
      │               │                   │               │
      │    H ≥ Hs     │                   │    H < Hs     │
──────┴───────────────┴──────          ───┴───────────────┴───

Full buoyancy credit                    Partial buoyancy credit
E = S                                  E < S

Dependence on superstructure height

Yes. The effective length depends directly on actual height if that height is below standard.

For an enclosed superstructure other than a raised quarterdeck:

E=S(HHs)if H<Hs \boxed{ E=S\left(\frac{H}{H_s}\right) \qquad \text{if } H < H_s } E=S(Hs​H​)if H<Hs​​

where:

  • SSS = actual length,
  • HHH = actual least height at side,
  • HsH_sHs​ = standard superstructure height.

If:

H≥Hs H\geq H_s H≥Hs​

then:

E=S \boxed{E=S} E=S​

This proportional reduction is specifically reflected in load-line rules: if height is less than HsH_sHs​, effective length equals actual length multiplied by the ratio of actual height to standard height. laws-lois.justice.gc

Example: ordinary enclosed superstructure

Given:

L=150 m L=150\,\text{m} L=150mS=90 m S=90\,\text{m} S=90mH=1.80 m H=1.80\,\text{m} H=1.80m

First calculate standard height:

Hs=1.80+150300=2.30 m H_s=1.80+\frac{150}{300}=2.30\,\text{m} Hs​=1.80+300150​=2.30m

Because:

H<Hs H<H_s H<Hs​E=90(1.802.30) E=90\left(\frac{1.80}{2.30}\right) E=90(2.301.80​)E=70.43 m E=70.43\,\text{m} E=70.43mE≈70.4 m \boxed{E\approx70.4\,\text{m}} E≈70.4m​

Although the actual deckhouse is 90 m long, only 70.4 m is credited in calculating the freeboard deduction.

Raised quarterdeck

A raised quarterdeck is treated more conservatively because it often has reduced height and a different contribution to reserve buoyancy. Its credit is limited; in typical Convention-form rules, the effective length is restricted to no more than 0.6L0.6L0.6L, and height conditions are more restrictive than for an ordinary enclosed superstructure. laws-lois.justice.gc

Link to freeboard deduction

The total effective length enters the superstructure/trunk deduction through the ratio:

EL \frac{E}{L} LE​

For example:

Small E/L → little protected buoyancy → small freeboard deduction
Large E/L → much protected buoyancy → larger freeboard deduction
E/L = 1 → maximum superstructure-related deduction

For a vessel where total effective enclosed-superstructure length equals the ship’s full Convention length, the maximum deduction is available. Where E<LE<LE<L, the deduction is calculated from a reduced relation based on E/LE/LE/L. laws-lois.justice.gc

Exam-ready summary

  • Tabular freeboard is selected from the Type A or Type B table using Convention length.
  • It is adjusted for: ship length below 100 m, block coefficient, depth, deck-line position, enclosed superstructures/trunks and sheer.
  • It is then checked against the minimum freeboard and minimum bow-height requirements.
  • Sheer is the rise of the freeboard deck at side from midships to the ends; it improves reserve buoyancy, reduces deck wetness and gives protection against green seas and downflooding.
  • Excess sheer earns a deduction; deficient sheer requires an addition.
  • Effective superstructure length is not necessarily the actual length: a low superstructure earns only proportionate credit because it supplies less protected buoyancy.
  • For a normal enclosed superstructure below standard height:
E=SHHs \boxed{E=S\frac{H}{H_s}} E=SHs​H​​
  • The greater the effective length EEE, the greater the permitted deduction from tabular freeboard—subject always to minimum safety limits.

M(x)=∫0x7.848(6x+x22)dx=7.848[3x2+x36]M(x) = \int_{0}^{x} 7.848 \left( 6x + \frac{x^2}{2} \right) dx = 7.848 \left[ 3x^2 + \frac{x^3}{6} \right]M(x)=∫0x​7.848(6x+2x2​)dx=7.848[3x2+6x3​]

Q.1 (b) Bilged Compartment Draft and GM

Given:

Step 1: Lost Buoyancy Method for New Draft

Q.2 (a) Simpson’s First and Second Rules Derivation

  • Simpson’s First Rule (1-4-1): Assumes the curve between 3 ordinates (2 intervals) is a second-degree polynomial y=a+bx+cx2y = a + bx + cx^2y=a+bx+cx2. Integrating this equation from −h-h−h to +h+h+h yields the area formula: Area=h3(y0+4y1+y2)\text{Area} = \frac{h}{3} (y_0 + 4y_1 + y_2)Area=3h​(y0​+4y1​+y2​) For nnn intervals (where nnn is even), it extends to: h3(y0+4y1+2y2+4y3+...+yn)\frac{h}{3} (y_0 + 4y_1 + 2y_2 + 4y_3 + ... + y_n)3h​(y0​+4y1​+2y2​+4y3​+...+yn​).
  • Simpson’s Second Rule (1-3-3-1): Assumes the curve between 4 ordinates (3 intervals) is a third-degree polynomial y=a+bx+cx2+dx3y = a + bx + cx^2 + dx^3y=a+bx+cx2+dx3. Integrating this from −1.5h-1.5h−1.5h to +1.5h+1.5h+1.5h yields: Area=3h8(y0+3y1+3y2+y3)\text{Area} = \frac{3h}{8} (y_0 + 3y_1 + 3y_2 + y_3)Area=83h​(y0​+3y1​+3y2​+y3​)

Q.2 (b) Moment of Inertia about y-axis

Consider a vertical strip of width dxdxdx and height yyy at a distance xxx from the y-axis.

  • Area of the strip, dA=y⋅dxdA = y \cdot dxdA=y⋅dx
  • The Moment of Inertia (MI) of this strip about the y-axis is dIy=x2⋅dAdI_y = x^2 \cdot dAdIy​=x2⋅dA
  • Substituting dAdAdA: dIy=x2⋅y⋅dxdI_y = x^2 \cdot y \cdot dxdIy​=x2⋅y⋅dx
  • Integrating over the entire curve: Iy=∫yx2dxI_y = \int y x^2 dxIy​=∫yx2dx

Q.3 Interrelationship of Hull Girder Terms

  • Bending Moment (M): The internal algebraic sum of moments resisting external loads (weights and buoyancies).
  • Neutral Axis (NA): The longitudinal axis within the ship’s cross-section where the bending stress is zero. It passes through the centroid of the section.
  • Second Moment of Area (I): Also called Moment of Inertia. It is the geometric property ∫y2dA\int y^2 dA∫y2dA measuring the section’s resistance to bending.
  • Section Modulus (Z): Defined as Z=I/ymaxZ = I / y_{max}Z=I/ymax​, where ymaxy_{max}ymax​ is the distance from the NA to the outermost fiber (deck or keel).
  • Bending Stress (σ\sigmaσ): The stress induced by the bending moment, calculated using the Engineer’s Bending Equation: σ=MZ=M⋅yI\sigma = \frac{M}{Z} = \frac{M \cdot y}{I}σ=ZM​=IM⋅y​.
  • Hull Deflection: The physical sagging or hogging deformation of the hull girder. It is mathematically linked to BM via the differential equation: EId2zdx2=MEI \frac{d^2z}{dx^2} = MEIdx2d2z​=M, where EEE is Young’s Modulus.
  • Interrelationship: External loads create a Bending Moment (M). The hull girder resists this via its Second Moment of Area (I) and Section Modulus (Z), which dictates the maximum Bending Stress (σ\sigmaσ) at the deck/keel. If the stress exceeds the yield strength, permanent Hull Deflection or failure occurs.

Step 4: Thrust per unit area (c)

  • Blade Area AB=BAR×πD24=0.45×π×5.824=11.889 m2A_B = \text{BAR} \times \frac{\pi D^2}{4} = 0.45 \times \frac{\pi \times 5.8^2}{4} = 11.889 \text{ m}^2AB​=BAR×4πD2​=0.45×4π×5.82​=11.889 m2
  • Thrust T=TPVa=38006.610=574.88 kNT = \frac{TP}{V_a} = \frac{3800}{6.610} = 574.88 \text{ kN}T=Va​TP​=6.6103800​=574.88 kN
  • Thrust per unit area = 574.8811.889=48.35 kN/m2\frac{574.88}{11.889} = \mathbf{48.35 \text{ kN/m}^2}11.889574.88​=48.35 kN/m2

Step 5: Torque delivered (d)

  • ηP=TP2πNQ  ⟹  Q=38002π×2×0.64=472.49 kNm\eta_P = \frac{TP}{2 \pi N Q} \implies Q = \frac{3800}{2 \pi \times 2 \times 0.64} = \mathbf{472.49 \text{ kNm}}ηP​=2πNQTP​⟹Q=2π×2×0.643800​=472.49 kNm

Q.5 (a) Ship Resistance from Model Test

Given: Model Lm=6L_m=6Lm​=6 m, Sm=7S_m=7Sm​=7 m², Vm=3V_m=3Vm​=3 kts (1.5431.5431.543 m/s), Rtm=35R_{tm}=35Rtm​=35 N. Ship Ls=120L_s=120Ls​=120 m. n=1.825n=1.825n=1.825, SCF=1.15.

  • Scale ratio λ=120/6=20\lambda = 120 / 6 = 20λ=120/6=20.
  • Ship speed Vs=Vmλ=3×20=13.416 knots=6.90 m/sV_s = V_m \sqrt{\lambda} = 3 \times \sqrt{20} = 13.416 \text{ knots} = 6.90 \text{ m/s}Vs​=Vm​λ​=3×20​=13.416 knots=6.90 m/s.

Q.5 (b) Frictional Resistance Dependencies

  1. Length of Ship: Directly increases the wetted surface area. It also affects the Reynolds number, altering the frictional coefficient CfC_fCf​.
  2. Ship’s Speed: Frictional resistance is proportional to VnV^nVn (where n≈1.825n \approx 1.825n≈1.825 according to Froude, or roughly V2V^2V2 in turbulent flow).
  3. Wetted Surface Area: Directly proportional; a larger surface area yields higher total frictional drag.
  4. Hull Roughness: Increases the thickness of the viscous sublayer and disrupts the boundary layer, significantly increasing the frictional resistance coefficient over time due to corrosion, biofouling, and paint degradation.

Q.1 (b) Mono-hull vs. Multi-hull Ships

  • Comparison & Speed/Power Ratio: Mono-hulls have a single V-shaped or U-shaped hull, offering high cargo capacity but suffering from high wave-making resistance at high Froude numbers. Multi-hulls (catamarans, trimarans) consist of narrow demihulls. This narrowness drastically reduces wave-making resistance at high speeds, giving multi-hulls a vastly superior speed/power ratio for fast cruising.
  • Examples: Mono-hull (Container ships, VLCCs, conventional ferries). Multi-hull (High-speed crew boats, naval corvettes, luxury catamaran ferries).
  • Why Multi-hulls are smaller: Scaling up a multi-hull requires an exponentially wider beam to maintain stability, leading to immense torsional and transverse bending stresses on the cross-deck structure connecting the hulls. Furthermore, large multi-hulls exceed the dimensions of standard locks, drydocks, and port infrastructure, making them structurally and economically unviable for bulk cargo transport compared to mono-hulls.

Q.2 (a) Propeller Cavitation Terms

  1. Tip Cavitation: Occurs at the blade tips due to the high pressure differential between the face and back. Water flows around the tip, creating a low-pressure vortex core that vaporizes the water.
  2. Sheet Cavitation: Forms a continuous, stable sheet of vapor on the suction face (back) of the blade near the leading edge where the local pressure drops below the vapor pressure.
  3. Spot (Bubble) Cavitation: Occurs as isolated, unstable vapor bubbles on the blade surface, often triggered by local surface roughness, pitting, or specific pressure pockets rather than a continuous low-pressure zone.

Q.2 (b) Rolling Decrement

  • Decrement: The progressive reduction in the maximum angle of roll in each successive cycle when a ship rolls in still water after an initial disturbance.
  • Graph: An exponentially decaying sine wave (X-axis: Number of oscillations, Y-axis: Roll angle).
  • Causes of Amplitude Reduction:
    1. Frictional resistance of the hull (skin friction).
    2. Eddy-making resistance (form drag due to hull shape).
    3. Wave-making resistance (energy radiated away as generated waves).
    4. Lift forces on appendages (e.g., bilge keels, rudders, stabilizing fins).

Q.4 (b) Oil Tanker Hull Strengths vs. Dry Cargo

  • Stresses: Tankers feature a continuous, uninterrupted strength deck (no large hatch openings) and a deep double bottom. This provides a massive section modulus, offering superior resistance to global hogging and sagging bending moments compared to dry cargo ships.
  • Stability: The double bottom allows for very low KG (ballast tanks), yielding high initial GM. The centerline longitudinal bulkhead and wing tank arrangements provide excellent transverse stability and damage stability.
  • ILLC Considerations: Because of their inherent structural continuity and double-hull damage stability (mandated by MARPOL), tankers are often assigned Type ‘B’ freeboards, which can be slightly reduced compared to Type ‘A’ if strict damage stability criteria are met, maximizing cargo deadweight.

Q.5 (a) Submarine Hull Construction

  • Outer Hull: Constructed from lightweight, hydrodynamically optimized materials (e.g., low-carbon steel or fiberglass). Its stress/strain curve shows a lower yield strength, as it is designed purely to minimize drag and house sonar/sensors, not to withstand deep-sea pressure.
  • Inner (Pressure) Hull: Constructed from high-tensile steel (e.g., HY-80/HY-100). The stress/strain curve exhibits a very high yield point, high ultimate tensile strength, and high ductility. It is circular/cylindrical to distribute external hydrostatic pressure evenly as membrane stresses.
  • Negative Tank: A specialized tank used to precisely control the submarine’s buoyancy. By flooding it, the submarine overcomes positive buoyancy to dive or maintain a specific depth, compensating for weight changes (e.g., torpedo firing, fuel consumption).

Since sin⁡θ≠0\sin\theta \neq 0sinθ=0, the term in the bracket must be zero: GM+12BMtan⁡2θ=0  ⟹  tan⁡2θ=−2GMBMGM + \frac{1}{2} BM \tan^2\theta = 0 \implies \tan^2\theta = \frac{-2 GM}{BM}GM+21​BMtan2θ=0⟹tan2θ=BM−2GM​ tan⁡θ=−2GMBM\tan\theta = \sqrt{\frac{-2 GM}{BM}}tanθ=BM−2GM​​ (Note: GM is negative, making the root positive).

Practical Use for Timber Carrier: A 7-degree loll indicates a negative GM, likely caused by waterlogged timber deck cargo raising the VCG.

  • Action: The Master must NOT attempt to correct the list by shifting weights or ballasting the high side, as this will cause the ship to capsize.
  • Correction: The Master must lower the Center of Gravity (G). This is done by jettisoning timber cargo from the high side or pressing up/slack tanks low down on the low side to lower G without creating a free-surface moment.

Q.6 Safe Return to Port (SRtP) Regulations

The SRtP regulations (SOLAS II-1/2-1) mandate that large passenger ships (typically Ro-Ro and cruise ships >120m) must be designed to survive a casualty (fire or flooding) and safely return to port under their own power, avoiding the need for immediate, dangerous at-sea evacuation.

  • Robustness & Redundancy: Requires separation of essential systems (propulsion, steering, power) into multiple safe zones. If one zone is compromised, the ship retains enough power and steering to navigate to a safe haven.
  • Fire Safety: Mandates strict fire zoning (A-60 boundaries) and the ability to isolate the fire while maintaining a “safe area” for passengers.
  • Damage Stability: Ensures the ship remains afloat and stable with a limited heel angle (usually ≤10∘\le 10^\circ≤10∘) even after multiple compartment flooding, allowing for safe internal movement and preventing capsizing.
  • Impact on Design: Drives the integration of cross-flooding arrangements, multiple engine rooms, enhanced fire detection/suppression, and careful arrangement of muster stations to keep passengers safe during the transit back to port.

Q.1 (a) Importance of Bonjean Curves

Definition & Diagram: Bonjean curves are a set of curves plotted for each transverse section (station) of a ship. The X-axis represents the cross-sectional area of the immersed portion, and the Y-axis represents the draft. (Sketch: A ship profile with vertical lines at each station. On each vertical line, a curve is plotted showing Area vs. Draft.)

Importance and Applications:

  1. Longitudinal Strength in Waves: They are the primary tool for calculating the buoyancy distribution along the ship’s length when the vessel is in a wave. By superimposing the wave profile on the Bonjean curves, the exact immersed area at each station can be read, allowing for the calculation of Shear Forces and Bending Moments.
  2. Damage Stability & Floodable Length: They are used to quickly determine the buoyancy lost and the new waterline when a compartment is bilged, aiding in the calculation of floodable length curves.
  3. Trim and Stability Calculations: They allow for rapid estimation of displacement and Longitudinal Center of Buoyancy (LCB) for any arbitrary waterline (even when the ship is trimmed), which is crucial for loading and ballasting operations.

Q.1 (b) Screw Propeller Sketch

(Sketch Description: A 3D or 2D profile of a propeller blade attached to a central hub.)

  • Hub: The central cylindrical boss that connects the blades to the propeller shaft.
  • Blade Tip: The outermost extremity of the blade, tracing the maximum propeller diameter circle.
  • Blade Root: The inner edge of the blade where it merges into the hub.
  • Propeller Diameter: The total diameter of the circle traced by the blade tips (2×2 \times2× Radius).
  • Pressure Face: The face of the blade that pushes against the water to generate thrust (typically the aft-facing surface when moving ahead).
  • Suction Back: The face of the blade that experiences low pressure, drawing water in (typically the forward-facing surface). This is the face most susceptible to cavitation.

Q.2 (b) Effect on Curve of Static Stability

  1. Grain Cargo Shift:
    • Effect: Shifting grain to one side creates a permanent heeling moment. The GZ curve is effectively shifted to the right by the angle of list (θlist\theta_{list}θlist​).
    • Dynamical Stability: The area under the GZ curve (which represents dynamical stability) is significantly reduced because the maximum righting lever is reached at a smaller angle relative to the new vertical, and the range of stability is curtailed.
  2. Formation of Ice:
    • Effect: Ice accumulation adds weight high up on the ship (especially on masts, rigging, and exposed decks), raising the Vertical Center of Gravity (KG). This reduces the initial GM. The entire GZ curve is lowered, resulting in a reduced maximum GZ and a shorter range of stability.
    • Dynamical Stability: The total area under the curve (dynamical stability) is reduced, making the ship more vulnerable to capsizing in heavy seas.

Where ImassI_{mass}Imass​ is the mass moment of inertia, given by Imass=Δgkxx2I_{mass} = \frac{\Delta}{g} k_{xx}^2Imass​=gΔ​kxx2​ (kxxk_{xx}kxx​ is the radius of gyration). Substituting ImassI_{mass}Imass​:

Radius of Gyration (kxxk_{xx}kxx​): It is the theoretical distance from the axis of rotation (longitudinal axis) at which the entire mass of the ship could be concentrated to produce the same mass moment of inertia as the actual distributed mass.

Q.6 (a) Submarine Surfacing and Submerging

Submerging: To dive, the submarine opens the main ballast tank (MBT) vents. Air escapes from the top of the tanks, and seawater floods in through the bottom flood ports, replacing the buoyant air. This reduces the ship’s overall buoyancy. Hydroplanes are angled to generate downward dynamic lift to assist the dive and control the bow’s pitch.

Surfacing: To surface, high-pressure air is blown into the MBTs, forcing the seawater out through the bottom flood ports. This restores positive buoyancy. Use of Hydroplanes in Early Surfacing: As buoyancy increases, the submarine might become unstable or the bow could dive due to hydrodynamic forces. Hydroplanes are angled to generate upward dynamic lift, helping the submarine break the surface cleanly, maintain a positive angle of attack, and prevent the bow from plunging back into the water before the MBTs are fully blown.

Q.6 (b) Alternative Intact Stability Criteria for Timber Carriers

IS Code 2008 Criteria:

  1. Initial GM: ≥0.15\ge 0.15≥0.15 m (or as per specific timber deck cargo calculations).
  2. Area under GZ curve: ≥0.08\ge 0.08≥0.08 m.rad up to an angle of 40∘40^\circ40∘.
  3. Maximum GZ: ≥0.25\ge 0.25≥0.25 m.
  4. Range of Stability: ≥25∘\ge 25^\circ≥25∘.

Reasons for Changed Criteria: Timber deck cargo provides additional buoyancy when submerged, which can increase the range of stability. However, it also adds significant weight high up (reducing GM), is susceptible to water absorption (increasing weight over time), and can shift if not properly secured. The criteria are specifically tailored to ensure the vessel has enough residual stability to counteract these adverse effects and the risk of cargo shift.

Prerequisites: To be eligible for this alternative criteria, the ship must:

  1. Comply with the International Convention on Load Lines (ICLL) regarding Timber Load Lines.
  2. Have the timber cargo stowed upright and securely lashed.
  3. The cargo must not extend forward of the superstructure or aft of the aft superstructure (if fitted).

Q.1 (b) Hydrodynamic Interactions

  1. Ship and River Bank (Bank Effect):
    • Causes: As a ship moves in a narrow channel, the restricted waterway between the ship and the bank causes water velocity to increase. According to Bernoulli’s theorem, this increases dynamic pressure and drops static pressure, creating a suction force that pulls the bow toward the bank and pushes the stern away, causing a sudden sheer.
    • Remedies: Reduce speed, maintain a safe distance from the bank, and apply proactive helm toward the bank to counteract the bow suction.
  2. Ship and Sea Bottom (Squat Effect):
    • Causes: In shallow water, the flow of water under the hull is restricted, increasing velocity and decreasing pressure. This causes the ship to sink deeper (squat) and often change trim.
    • Remedies: Reduce speed (squat is proportional to the square of the speed), calculate under-keel clearance dynamically, and be aware of trim changes.

Q.2 (a) Ship Wave Pattern and Interference

  • Wave Pattern: A moving ship generates two primary wave systems: Transverse waves (moving at the ship’s speed) and Divergent waves (angling outward at roughly 19.5° to the ship’s path, forming the Kelvin wake).
  • Interference: The bow and stern each generate their own wave systems. When these systems overlap, they interfere. If a bow crest meets a stern crest, they amplify each other (Hump). If a bow trough meets a stern crest, they cancel out (Hollow).
  • Humps and Hollows: These occur in the wave-making resistance curve against V/LV/\sqrt{L}V/L​ due to this interference. Humps (high resistance) occur when the systems are in phase; hollows (low resistance) occur when they are out of phase.
  • Approximate Values: The first major hump occurs at V/L≈0.3V/\sqrt{L} \approx 0.3V/L​≈0.3, and the first hollow occurs around V/L≈0.4V/\sqrt{L} \approx 0.4V/L​≈0.4 to 0.50.50.5.

Q.4 (a) Virtual Gravity and Virtual Upright

  • Virtual Gravity: On a trochoidal wave, water particles move in circular orbits, creating a centrifugal force. The vector sum of the true downward gravity and this centrifugal force creates an effective “virtual gravity” that is always perpendicular to the wave surface.
  • Virtual Upright: The ship’s plumb bob will hang perpendicular to the wave surface. This direction is the “virtual upright.” The ship will heel relative to this virtual upright, not the true vertical.
  • r and R: ‘R’ is the radius of the wave profile (epicycle), and ‘r’ is the radius of the water particle’s orbit at a given depth. r<Rr < Rr<R below the surface. At the crest, centrifugal force opposes gravity (reducing virtual gravity); at the trough, it adds to gravity.
  • Dangerous Conditions: For small vessels like fishing boats, if the wave length is close to the ship’s length, the rapid change in virtual gravity and transverse GM at the wave crest can cause a sudden loss of stability, leading to a sudden, catastrophic capsize (often associated with parametric rolling or pure loss of stability).

Q.4 (b) Parametric Rolling

  • Reasons: Ships with fine bows and full sterns experience massive fluctuations in waterplane area (and thus transverse GM) as waves pass along the hull. GM is lowest when a wave crest is at midships and highest when a trough is at midships.
  • Relationship: If this periodic change in GM occurs at a frequency that matches the ship’s natural roll frequency, it pumps energy into the roll. This happens when the Encounter Period (TET_ETE​) is exactly half the Natural Rolling Period (TRT_RTR​), i.e., TR=2×TET_R = 2 \times T_ETR​=2×TE​.

Q.5 (a) Submarine Systems

  1. Trimming Tanks: Located at the extreme forward and aft ends. They are used to transfer water to adjust the longitudinal center of gravity, ensuring the submarine remains level (neutral trim) during maneuvering and speed changes.
  2. Hull Buoyancy after Torpedo Ejection: Firing a torpedo removes significant weight, making the sub positively buoyant. To compensate, water is immediately flooded into the torpedo room or a dedicated compensation tank to replace the lost weight.
  3. Depth Compensation Tank: As a submarine dives, hydrostatic pressure compresses the hull, reducing its volume and buoyancy. This tank automatically or manually admits seawater to compensate for the “hull squeeze,” maintaining neutral buoyancy at depth.

Q.5 (b) Planing Hull Boats

  • Hydrodynamic Lift: A hard chine hull generates lift dynamically. As the boat moves forward, the flat bottom pushes water downward. By Newton’s third law, the water pushes the hull upward. The hard chine prevents water from spilling up the sides, concentrating the lift force under the flat bottom.
  • Poor Seakeeping: Because the hull is flat, it does not slice through waves. Instead, it “slams” onto the water surface, causing severe vertical accelerations, structural shock, and a very rough, uncomfortable ride for passengers in any chop.

Q.6 (a) Derivation of Attwood’s Formula

  1. Consider a ship heeled to a large angle θ\thetaθ. The emerged wedge (volume vvv) on the lowered side and the immersed wedge on the raised side must have equal volumes to maintain the same displacement.
  2. The center of buoyancy shifts from BBB to B1B_1B1​ because the volume of the emerged wedge has effectively been “moved” to the immersed wedge.
  3. Let yyy be the transverse distance of a small volume element vvv from the centerline axis. When moved from the emerged to the immersed wedge, its transverse shift is 2y2y2y.
  4. The total transverse moment of the shifted buoyancy is ∫v⋅(2y)\int v \cdot (2y)∫v⋅(2y).
  5. The transverse shift of the center of buoyancy (BB1cos⁡θBB_1 \cos\thetaBB1​cosθ) is this total moment divided by the total displaced volume (∇\nabla∇).
  6. From the geometry of the heeled ship, the righting lever GZ=(BB1cos⁡θ)−BGsin⁡θGZ = (BB_1 \cos\theta) - BG \sin\thetaGZ=(BB1​cosθ)−BGsinθ.
  7. Substituting the moment, we get Attwood’s Formula: GZ=∫v⋅2y∇−BGsin⁡θGZ = \frac{\int v \cdot 2y}{\nabla} - BG \sin\thetaGZ=∇∫v⋅2y​−BGsinθ

Q.6 (b) Limitations of the Wall-Sided Formula

  • Limitations: The formula GZ=sin⁡θ(GM+12BMtan⁡2θ)GZ = \sin\theta (GM + \frac{1}{2} BM \tan^2\theta)GZ=sinθ(GM+21​BMtan2θ) strictly assumes that the ship’s sides are perfectly vertical (wall-sided) at the waterline.
  • Relevance to “Wall” Sides: At large angles of heel, the deck edge will inevitably immerse, or the bilge will emerge. The waterplane is no longer bounded by vertical sides, completely invalidating the geometric assumptions of the formula.
  • Why use other formulas: For small angles (<10∘<10^\circ<10∘), the waterplane shape barely changes, and the metacenter MMM is fixed, making GZ=GMsin⁡θGZ = GM \sin\thetaGZ=GMsinθ perfectly acceptable. At large angles, MMM moves significantly, and the waterplane shape changes drastically. Therefore, we must use cross curves of stability (derived from the actual 3D hull form at each angle) or Attwood’s formula to accurately capture the true righting lever.

Q.3 2005 ILLC Amendments for Type B Ships

  • (a) Bow Height: The 2005 amendments introduced stricter minimum bow height requirements to prevent green water on deck. For Type B ships (like bulk carriers), this ensures the forward hatch covers are not subjected to catastrophic dynamic wave impact loads, significantly reducing the risk of water ingress and subsequent loss of stability.
  • (b) Hatch Cover Design: The amendments mandated higher design loads for hatch covers, requiring them to withstand increased sea pressures and dynamic loads. This forced an increase in scantlings, improved securing devices, and better weathertightness. Since water ingress through failed hatch covers is the primary cause of bulk carrier losses, this amendment directly enhances structural survivability in heavy weather.

(b) Hydrofoil Stability

  • Surface-Piercing Foils: V-shaped foils that pierce the water surface. When the craft heels, the immersed area of the lower foil increases (generating more lift), while the higher foil’s area decreases. This differential lift creates a strong passive righting moment.
  • Submerged Foils: Fully submerged foils rely on a dihedral angle for passive stability or an active electronic control system that adjusts the angle of attack to generate corrective lift forces when heel is detected.

(c) Limitations of GM

  1. GM only defines initial stability (small angles <10∘<10^\circ<10∘) and does not indicate the maximum righting lever (GZ max) or the angle at which it occurs.
  2. A ship with a large GM may have a short range of stability and low dynamical stability (small area under the GZ curve), making it prone to capsizing despite feeling “stiff”.
  3. GM fails to account for large-angle stability phenomena like deck edge immersion, freeboard loss, or the development of an angle of loll.

Q.6 Hull Failure and Drydocking

(a) Causes of Bulk Carrier Hull Failure (e.g., MV “Flare” / North Atlantic)

  1. Bending Moment in Ballast: In ballast, the ship experiences high still-water hogging. When combined with wave-induced sagging moments in heavy seas, it creates massive cyclic tensile and compressive stresses on the deck and bottom shell.
  2. Upkeep of Topside Tanks: Corrosion in the topside (hopper) tanks reduces the section modulus of the hull girder, particularly at the deck and upper bilge strakes, creating localized weak points susceptible to cracking.
  3. Resonant Rolling: Parametric or synchronous rolling in head or following seas can induce massive dynamic loads on the hull structure, rapidly propagating existing fatigue cracks.
  4. Brittle Fracture: The freezing waters of the North Atlantic can drop the hull steel below its ductile-to-brittle transition temperature. Combined with high tensile stresses and existing corrosion/fatigue cracks, this leads to sudden, catastrophic brittle fracture of the hull girder without warning.

(b) Virtual Loss of GM in Drydock Diagram Description: A midship cross-section resting on keel blocks.

  • Vectors: Gravity (WWW) acts downwards through GGG. Buoyancy (BBB) acts upwards through BBB. Upthrust (PPP) from the blocks acts upwards at the keel (KKK).
  • Derivation: When the ship heels by a small angle θ\thetaθ, the upthrust PPP at the keel creates a listing moment. The horizontal shift of the keel is KMsin⁡θKM \sin\thetaKMsinθ.
    • Listing Moment = P×KMsin⁡θP \times KM \sin\thetaP×KMsinθ
    • The ship’s natural Righting Moment = W×GMsin⁡θW \times GM \sin\thetaW×GMsinθ
    • Effective Righting Moment = W×GMsin⁡θ−P×KMsin⁡θ=(W×GM−P×KM)sin⁡θW \times GM \sin\theta - P \times KM \sin\theta = (W \times GM - P \times KM) \sin\thetaW×GMsinθ−P×KMsinθ=(W×GM−P×KM)sinθ

Q.1 Second-Generation Intact Stability Criteria

(a) Stability Failure Modes and Vulnerability Checks The IMO’s second-generation intact stability criteria (SGISC) address five specific dynamic stability failure modes that were not adequately covered by the current weather criterion:

  1. Parametric Rolling: Large roll angles induced by periodic variations in transverse stability (GM) in head or following seas.
  2. Pure Loss of Stability: Sudden capsize due to a significant reduction in GM when a wave crest is at midships.
  3. Surf-Riding and Broaching-to: Loss of control in following seas when the ship is caught by a wave and accelerated to wave speed, leading to a yaw and capsize.
  4. Dead Ship Condition: Loss of stability and subsequent capsize of a vessel drifting in beam seas after a propulsion failure.
  5. Excessive Acceleration: High vertical accelerations in head seas that can cause structural damage or injury to crew/passengers.

Formalized Procedures: For each mode, the criteria establish a formalized vulnerability check. Level 1 checks are simple, criteria-based thresholds. If a vessel fails Level 1, it undergoes a more rigorous Level 2 check, which uses advanced hydrodynamic simulations or simplified empirical formulas to assess the actual probability or severity of the failure mode in specific sea states.

(b) Impact on Coastal Shipping Small coastal vessels often lack the detailed hydrodynamic data (like extensive model test results) required for the complex Level 2 assessments. The impact includes:

  • Compliance Burden: Smaller operators may face high costs to generate the necessary data or perform numerical simulations.
  • Design Changes: Vessels might need hull form modifications (e.g., adding bilge keels or changing bow flare) to pass the vulnerability checks.
  • Operational Restrictions: If a vessel cannot meet the criteria, it may face strict weather windows or route restrictions, impacting its operational viability.

Q.2 Safe Return to Port (SRtP) and Industrial Personnel (IP) Code

(a) Evaluation of Safe Return to Port (SRtP)

  • Applicability: SRtP (SOLAS II-1/2-1) applies to passenger ships (especially Ro-Ro and cruise ships) of 120 m in length or more, built after 2010. It mandates that after a casualty (fire or flooding), the ship must retain essential systems to return to port without external assistance.
  • Effect on Costing & Operations: It significantly increases initial capital expenditure due to the need for redundant systems (multiple engine rooms, separated power grids), enhanced fire zoning (A-60 boundaries), and dedicated “safe areas.” Operationally, it requires rigorous crew training, complex emergency drills, and strict maintenance of redundant systems.
  • Passenger Capacity: While dedicated safe areas and redundant machinery spaces consume valuable volume, the SRtP framework sometimes allows for a relaxation of strict evacuation time limits, potentially enabling higher passenger capacities on certain deck configurations compared to traditional SOLAS requirements.

(b) Submissions to IMO SDC regarding >12 Industrial Personnel (IP) As a shipowner, my submissions to balance safety with operational feasibility would include:

  1. Safety Equipment (LSA & FFE): While IPs are not crew, they are not traditional passengers either. I would propose that LSA and fire-fighting equipment meet cargo ship standards but scaled to the maximum number of IPs, rather than the full, costly passenger ship (SOLAS) standards.
  2. Training and Familiarization: IPs often lack basic maritime safety training. I would submit that a mandatory, simplified “Basic Safety Induction” must be conducted before departure, covering muster stations, immersion suits, and basic fire awareness.
  3. Medical Facilities: Offshore personnel are prone to industrial injuries. The code should mandate a dedicated medical room with telemedicine capabilities, rather than just standard passenger ship medical facilities.
  4. Chain of Command: The code must explicitly state that the Master retains absolute authority over the vessel’s safety and navigation, preventing conflicts between the offshore installation manager and the ship’s Master during emergencies.

  • Allowable point load PPP for a simply supported beam with a midspan point load: Mmax=P⋅L4  ⟹  σ=MZ=P⋅L/4b⋅h2/6=1.5⋅P⋅Lb⋅h2M_{max} = \frac{P \cdot L}{4} \implies \sigma = \frac{M}{Z} = \frac{P \cdot L / 4}{b \cdot h^2 / 6} = \frac{1.5 \cdot P \cdot L}{b \cdot h^2}Mmax​=4P⋅L​⟹σ=ZM​=b⋅h2/6P⋅L/4​=b⋅h21.5⋅P⋅L​ P=σallow⋅b⋅h21.5⋅L=55×100×10021.5×750=48,888 N≈48.89 kN (or 4.98 T)P = \frac{\sigma_{allow} \cdot b \cdot h^2}{1.5 \cdot L} = \frac{55 \times 100 \times 100^2}{1.5 \times 750} = \mathbf{48,888 \text{ N} \approx 48.89 \text{ kN} \text{ (or 4.98 T)}}P=1.5⋅Lσallow​⋅b⋅h2​=1.5×75055×100×1002​=48,888 N≈48.89 kN (or 4.98 T)
  • Allowable load for this contact condition = 1.5×4.98=7.47 Tonnes1.5 \times 4.98 = \mathbf{7.47 \text{ Tonnes}}1.5×4.98=7.47 Tonnes.
  • Number of dunnage pieces required per coil = 20 T7.47 T=2.67  ⟹  3 pieces\frac{20 \text{ T}}{7.47 \text{ T}} = 2.67 \implies \mathbf{3 \text{ pieces}}7.47 T20 T​=2.67⟹3 pieces.

Step 3: Check Deflection

  • Limiting deflection = 750 mm375=2 mm\frac{750 \text{ mm}}{375} = \mathbf{2 \text{ mm}}375750 mm​=2 mm.
  • Actual deflection δ=P⋅L348⋅E⋅I=48888×750348×10350×(100×1003/12)=0.0049 mm\delta = \frac{P \cdot L^3}{48 \cdot E \cdot I} = \frac{48888 \times 750^3}{48 \times 10350 \times (100 \times 100^3 / 12)} = \mathbf{0.0049 \text{ mm}}δ=48⋅E⋅IP⋅L3​=48×10350×(100×1003/12)48888×7503​=0.0049 mm.
  • 0.0049 mm≪2 mm0.0049 \text{ mm} \ll 2 \text{ mm}0.0049 mm≪2 mm (Safe).

Answers: (a) Type and Size: Hard Wood dunnage, 100 mm×100 mm100 \text{ mm} \times 100 \text{ mm}100 mm×100 mm cross-section. (b) Length of Dunnage: Must be at least the width of the coil. Specify 1.6 m1.6 \text{ m}1.6 m (or 1.8 m1.8 \text{ m}1.8 m to allow for lashing/overhang). (c) Distribution: Place 3 pieces of 100×100×1600 mm100 \times 100 \times 1600 \text{ mm}100×100×1600 mm Hard Wood dunnage transversely under the coil, spaced evenly along the 1.6 m1.6 \text{ m}1.6 m length (approx. 0.53 m0.53 \text{ m}0.53 m apart). (d) Variation across holds: Dunnage requirements may vary if the tank top frame spacing differs between holds, or if the local deck strength (allowable load per m2m^2m2) is lower in certain holds, requiring more pieces of dunnage or larger scantlings to distribute the load.

Q.5 National Waterway Tanker Design

(a) Mid-Ship Section and Main Dimensions

  • Payload (DWT): 2400 T2400 \text{ T}2400 T
  • Draft Restriction: The most restrictive Least Available Depth (LAD) is 2.5 m2.5 \text{ m}2.5 m. Assuming an Under-Keel Clearance (UKC) of 0.4 m0.4 \text{ m}0.4 m, the maximum operational draft is 2.1 m2.1 \text{ m}2.1 m.
  • Main Dimensions:
    • Length (LLL) = 110 m110 \text{ m}110 m (Max permitted)
    • Breadth (BBB) = 12 m12 \text{ m}12 m (Max permitted)
    • Draft (TTT) = 2.1 m2.1 \text{ m}2.1 m
    • Depth (DDD) = 3.0 m3.0 \text{ m}3.0 m (Provides adequate freeboard and clearance for overhead bridges).
  • Block Coefficient (CbC_bCb​): 2400110×12×2.1×1.0 (fresh water)=0.865\frac{2400}{110 \times 12 \times 2.1 \times 1.0 \text{ (fresh water)}} = 0.865110×12×2.1×1.0 (fresh water)2400​=0.865 (Typical for a river tanker).
  • Mid-Ship Section Description: A double-bottom structure (to protect against grounding in shallow waterways), single deck with longitudinal framing, transverse side frames, and a centerline longitudinal bulkhead (or double side skins if pollution regulations mandate it).
  • Factors Considered: LAD constraints (dictating draft), topography/lock constraints (dictating beam), overhead bridges (dictating air draft/depth), payload requirement, and structural integrity for shallow water navigation.

(b) Engine Power Evaluation

  • Speed (VVV): 2 knots=1.029 m/s2 \text{ knots} = 1.029 \text{ m/s}2 knots=1.029 m/s.
  • Wetted Surface Area (SSS): Approx. L×(B+2T)×0.9=110×(12+4.2)×0.9≈1600 m2L \times (B + 2T) \times 0.9 = 110 \times (12 + 4.2) \times 0.9 \approx 1600 \text{ m}^2L×(B+2T)×0.9=110×(12+4.2)×0.9≈1600 m2.
  • Frictional Resistance (RfR_fRf​):
    • Reynolds number Re=1.029×1101.19×10−6≈9.5×107Re = \frac{1.029 \times 110}{1.19 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 9.5 \times 10^7Re=1.19×10−61.029×110​≈9.5×107.
    • Cf=0.075(log⁡10Re−2)2≈0.00155C_f = \frac{0.075}{(\log_{10} Re - 2)^2} \approx 0.00155Cf​=(log10​Re−2)20.075​≈0.00155.
    • Rf=0.5×1000×1600×1.0292×0.00155≈1315 NR_f = 0.5 \times 1000 \times 1600 \times 1.029^2 \times 0.00155 \approx 1315 \text{ N}Rf​=0.5×1000×1600×1.0292×0.00155≈1315 N.
  • Total Resistance (RtR_tRt​): At this extremely low Froude number (Fn≈0.03Fn \approx 0.03Fn≈0.03), wave-making resistance is negligible. Assuming residual resistance is 20%20\%20% of RfR_fRf​ and adding a 15%15\%15% correlation allowance:
    • Rt≈1.15×1.2×1315≈1815 NR_t \approx 1.15 \times 1.2 \times 1315 \approx 1815 \text{ N}Rt​≈1.15×1.2×1315≈1815 N.
  • Effective Power (PEP_EPE​): Rt×V=1815×1.029≈1867 W=1.87 kWR_t \times V = 1815 \times 1.029 \approx 1867 \text{ W} = \mathbf{1.87 \text{ kW}}Rt​×V=1815×1.029≈1867 W=1.87 kW.
  • Shaft Power (PSP_SPS​): Assuming a low propulsive efficiency (ηD≈0.45\eta_D \approx 0.45ηD​≈0.45) due to the low speed and small propeller:
    • PS=1.870.45≈4.15 kWP_S = \frac{1.87}{0.45} \approx \mathbf{4.15 \text{ kW}}PS​=0.451.87​≈4.15 kW.
  • Conclusion: A very small engine, such as a 5 kW to 10 kW diesel or electric motor, is more than sufficient to propel this vessel at 2 knots.

Q.6 Change in GM for Connected Hulls

Given: Single hull Δ=248 t\Delta = 248 \text{ t}Δ=248 t, TPC=0.5TPC = 0.5TPC=0.5, GM=0.4 mGM = 0.4 \text{ m}GM=0.4 m. Distance between centerlines = 7 m7 \text{ m}7 m.

Step 1: Understand the New Configuration When the two identical hulls are connected by a weightless platform:

  • New Displacement Δnew=2×248=496 t\Delta_{new} = 2 \times 248 = 496 \text{ t}Δnew​=2×248=496 t.
  • Since the platform is weightless, the vertical center of gravity remains unchanged: KGnew=KGKG_{new} = KGKGnew​=KG.
  • The draft of each hull remains unchanged, so the vertical center of buoyancy remains unchanged: KBnew=KBKB_{new} = KBKBnew​=KB.

Step 2: Calculate the New Transverse Moment of Inertia (InewI_{new}Inew​) The new waterplane consists of the two individual waterplanes. The new centerline is exactly midway between the two hulls, so the distance from each hull’s centerline to the new centerline is d=72=3.5 md = \frac{7}{2} = 3.5 \text{ m}d=27​=3.5 m. Using the parallel axis theorem:

Inew=2×(Iorig+Awp⋅d2)I_{new} = 2 \times (I_{orig} + A_{wp} \cdot d^2)Inew​=2×(Iorig​+Awp​⋅d2)

Step 3: Calculate the New BM

BMnew=Inew∇new=2×(Iorig+Awp⋅d2)2×∇=Iorig∇+Awp⋅d2∇=BMorig+Awp⋅d2∇BM_{new} = \frac{I_{new}}{\nabla_{new}} = \frac{2 \times (I_{orig} + A_{wp} \cdot d^2)}{2 \times \nabla} = \frac{I_{orig}}{\nabla} + \frac{A_{wp} \cdot d^2}{\nabla} = BM_{orig} + \frac{A_{wp} \cdot d^2}{\nabla}BMnew​=∇new​Inew​​=2×∇2×(Iorig​+Awp​⋅d2)​=∇Iorig​​+∇Awp​⋅d2​=BMorig​+∇Awp​⋅d2​

Step 4: Calculate the Change in GM Since KM=KB+BMKM = KB + BMKM=KB+BM, and both KBKBKB and KGKGKG are unchanged:

ΔGM=GMnew−GMorig=KMnew−KMorig=BMnew−BMorig=Awp⋅d2∇\Delta GM = GM_{new} - GM_{orig} = KM_{new} - KM_{orig} = BM_{new} - BM_{orig} = \frac{A_{wp} \cdot d^2}{\nabla}ΔGM=GMnew​−GMorig​=KMnew​−KMorig​=BMnew​−BMorig​=∇Awp​⋅d2​

We know that Awp=TPC×100ρA_{wp} = \frac{TPC \times 100}{\rho}Awp​=ρTPC×100​ and ∇=Δρ\nabla = \frac{\Delta}{\rho}∇=ρΔ​. Substituting these:

ΔGM=(TPC×100ρ)⋅d2(Δρ)=TPC×100×d2Δ\Delta GM = \frac{\left(\frac{TPC \times 100}{\rho}\right) \cdot d^2}{\left(\frac{\Delta}{\rho}\right)} = \frac{TPC \times 100 \times d^2}{\Delta}ΔGM=(ρΔ​)(ρTPC×100​)⋅d2​=ΔTPC×100×d2​

Step 5: Final Calculation

ΔGM=0.5×100×3.52248=50×12.25248=612.5248=2.47 m\Delta GM = \frac{0.5 \times 100 \times 3.5^2}{248} = \frac{50 \times 12.25}{248} = \frac{612.5}{248} = \mathbf{2.47 \text{ m}}ΔGM=2480.5×100×3.52​=24850×12.25​=248612.5​=2.47 m
